IEE Colloquium on Physical Characterisation of Polymeric Dielectrics
abstract: Polymers can withstand extremely high electric fields, in excess of 1000 MV m/sup -1/ yet low fields of a few MV m/sup -1/ may eventually cause breakdown in some polymer-insulated systems. Apparently identical insulating systems may, when tested, breakdown at widely differing voltages, or, in service, survive for widely differing periods. The talk will aim to identify the different physical mechanisms responsible for breakdown and degradation in polymers and briefly review some of the methods used for their characterization. Comments will be made on techniques used to assess the life of high-voltage polymeric power cables.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

abstract: A range of techniques have been used for the determination of the morphology of polyethylene. These include optical and transmission electron microscopy, differential scanning calorimetry and wide angle X-ray diffraction. Comprehensive X-ray diffraction studies have been carried out on sheet samples of polyethylene which have been cross-linked using radiation, peroxide and silane methods. In addition, cross-linked cable samples have been examined at room temperature and at 90 degrees C. Changes in polymer morphology with crosslinking and on heating will be discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Polymer characterization by dynamic mechanical thermal analysis and comparison with dielectric behaviour
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Physical Characterisation of Polymeric Dielectrics
abstract: Dynamic mechanical thermal analysis (DMTA) is now a well established technique for characterizing the basic performance properties of polymeric materials over a wide temperature range and a limited frequency range. The method operates via the molecular relaxation technique and not via heat capacity changes as in all forms of calorimetry. In the DMTA method an oscillating mechanical stress is imposed in order to probe the molecular relaxation processes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Spectroscopy and light scattering techniques in the study of solid dielectrics
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Physical Characterisation of Polymeric Dielectrics
abstract: The contribution will consider the application of infrared and Raman spectroscopy and elastic laser light scattering in understanding the chemical and physical characteristics of polymeric insulating materials. Such understanding is essential to any detailed assessment of the properties and performance of polymeric materials in service and in supporting laboratory studies.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Physical Characterisation of Polymeric Dielectrics
abstract: The amount of information that can be obtained about the relaxation process from a single measurement in either the time or frequency domain is limited. However by making use of another variable, such as temperature or pressure, further insight into the nature of the relaxation process can be gained. Published data from a number of sources for relaxation in polyethylene will be reported and it will be shown that the beta process of relaxation, commonly observed in the region of 200 K, can be associated with thermally assisted quantum mechanical tunnelling of protonic charges between close neighbour sites.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Charge and electric field distributions in solid dielectrics
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Physical Characterisation of Polymeric Dielectrics
abstract: It is useful to know precisely what field and charge distributions exist within polymer insulation, e.g. at electrical breakdown. Ultrasonic, Kerr effect, radiation methods, Stark spectroscopy, optical molecular probes, thermally stimulated currents and transient methods can be used to perform this task.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
